To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) Humans perform well in estimating the direction of gaze of others, even when the face is partially occluded and/or the eyes are not visible; 2) This ability is based on a computational representation of the eyes-region which is task-specific; 3) This representation is not based on the availability of input dynamic; 4) This representation is consistent with neurophysiological evidence for the existence of face regions in the brain that are specialized for processing specific tasks.
(i) humans are remarkably accurate in determining the gaze of others in real-life scenes, and (ii) the eyes-region contains sufficient information for this task.

humans are remarkably accurate at determining the direction of gaze of others in unconstrained conditions, and that the eyes-region, which contains the required information for gaze estimation, is processed differently in the brain compared to the rest of the face, even though the two are processed jointly.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the computational and perceptual mechanisms underlying the ability to interpret the gaze direction of another human being in a lifelike environment.
understanding the perceptual processes that enable humans to perceive and interpret the gaze of others in their surroundings.
the perceptual processes underlying the ability to interpret gaze direction in humans, and the computational principles underlying these processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
humans are remarkably accurate in determining the gaze of others in real-life situations, even when the eyes-region is the sole visible part of their face.
humans are remarkably good at estimating gaze direction in natural scenes, and that this capacity is based on the eyes-region alone.
humans are remarkably accurate in estimating gaze direction, and that the eyes-region, rather than the entire face, contains on its own the required information for this task.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that humans are remarkably accurate in perceiving the direction of gaze, even when the eyes region is the only available source of information, and we have developed a computational model that replicates this finding.
humans are very good at perceiving gaze direction in natural and unconstrained conditions, and that the eyes-region is the main source of information.
the eyes-region is the most informative part of the visual input when it comes to gaze perception in natural scenes.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the human visual system is able to use information from both the eyes-region and the head-region to estimate the direction of gaze of other individuals, and that this ability is based on a representation that is task-specific, and does not rely on the availability of input motion.

the perception of unconstrained gaze in natural scenes is a highly robust and reliable cognitive skill, which is supported by the eyes-region alone, and is mediated by a dedicated perceptual mechanism, which is distinct from other face processing mechanisms.
humans are remarkably good at estimating gaze direction in naturalistic scenes, and that the eyes-region is sufficient for this task.
